nameStory: The meadow fritillary gets its name from its love of open meadows and grasslands, where it dances among wildflowers on sunny days. "Fritillary" comes from the Latin word for dice cup, referring to the checkered pattern on many butterflies in this group, though our meadow friend shows this pattern more subtly than some of its flashier cousins.
description: The meadow fritillary is a medium-sized orange butterfly with a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches. Its wings display a warm orange-brown color decorated with darker spots and lines, creating a somewhat muted but beautiful pattern. Unlike some of the showier fritillaries, this species has a more understated elegance with less dramatic silver markings. You'll often see them flying low over grasses and flowers in open areas, with a somewhat erratic but purposeful flight pattern.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Orange-brown wings with darker brown spots and zigzag lines, but lacking the prominent silver spots on the underwing that many other fritillaries display

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a wingspan around 1.5-2 inches, noticeably smaller and more delicate than great spangled fritillaries you might see in the same areas

idTips.label: Flight Behavior
idTips.description: Flies with quick, somewhat jerky movements close to the ground, often pausing to nectar on low flowers like violets and asters

idTips.label: Underwing Appearance
idTips.description: When wings are closed, the underwing shows muted orange and brown tones without the flashy silver patches that distinguish many other fritillary species

idTips.label: Body and Antennae
idTips.description: Fuzzy orange-brown body with club-tipped black antennae that feel slightly rough to the touch if you're lucky enough to have one land on you

habitat: Look for meadow fritillaries in open grasslands, meadows, prairies, and field edges throughout New England, especially areas with plenty of native violets which serve as their caterpillar host plants. They prefer sunny locations with a mix of grasses and wildflowers, often in slightly moist areas near streams or in low-lying meadows. You'll also find them along power line cuts, old fields, and nature preserve grasslands from sea level up to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with the first fresh individuals appearing when violets and other early wildflowers are blooming. Look for them nectaring on spring flowers during warm, sunny afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through July when adults are most abundant and actively mating. This is the best time to spot them as they visit a variety of wildflowers for nectar.
seasonality.fall: A second generation may appear in late summer into early fall in warmer areas, though they're less common than the spring/early summer flight. Look for somewhat worn individuals into September.
seasonality.winter: Not active as adults; they overwinter as partially grown caterpillars tucked away in leaf litter and debris near violet plants, waiting for spring warmth to resume feeding.

funFact: Meadow fritillary caterpillars are picky eaters that will only munch on violets, but here's the twist: the mother butterfly doesn't lay her eggs directly on the violet plants! Instead, she scatters them randomly in the grass nearby, and the tiny caterpillars must find their own way to a violet plant or starve—it's like nature's ultimate treasure hunt for newborns.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the silver-bordered fritillary, but remember this simple trick: meadow fritillaries have 'modest meadow' underwings without flashy silver spots, while silver-bordered fritillaries live up to their name with prominent silvery patches on their underwings. If you see obvious silver bling when the wings are folded, it's not a meadow fritillary.
contextualKnowledge: Interestingly, there's a European butterfly that also goes by the name 'meadow fritillary,' which can cause confusion when reading about butterflies online or in books that cover multiple continents. Always check whether your source is talking about North American or European species to avoid mix-ups.
compareHints: Among its Boloria relatives in New England, the meadow fritillary is the most widespread and the one you're most likely to encounter in typical meadow habitats. The silver-bordered fritillary prefers wetter areas like bogs and has more prominent silver markings, while the bog fritillary is restricted to very specific acidic wetland habitats. The meadow fritillary's understated orange-brown coloring and lack of silver spots make it the most 'plain' of the group, but also the most adaptable to different grassland environments.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Boloria relatives in New England, the American Silver-bordered Fritillary is distinguished by its prominent silver hindwing spots, while the Meadow Fritillary lacks silver markings entirely.
Compared to other Boloria fritillaries in New England, the Arctic fritillary is the most cold-adapted and northern in distribution.
